beginner.headline: Dormouse Numbers May Be Rising in England and Wales
beginner.brief: Dormouse numbers in England and Wales may be going up after years of falling. A dormouse is a small animal like a mouse. The hazel dormouse is the only kind of dormouse in the UK. The new figures suggest there were almost 10 percent more dormice in 2025 than in 2020. But researchers say the real change could be quite different from what these figures show. There are still almost 60 percent fewer dormice than in 2000. Dormice sleep through the winter in nests on the ground. Scientists think dormice may spend less time in deep sleep in warmer summers. This may leave them with more energy to feed and have young. People who work to save dormice say we still need to protect the woods where they live.

intermediate.headline: Hazel Dormice May Be Recovering in England and Wales
intermediate.brief: Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline. The hazel dormouse is the only dormouse species in the UK, and it now lives mainly in southern England and parts of Wales. The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme has been tracking dormouse populations at sites in England and Wales since 1998. The programme found that dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60% since 2000. More recent results suggest that numbers rose by nearly 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers say the estimate is uncertain. This apparent rise came during a period when springs and summers were warmer and drier than average. In cold, wet weather or when food is scarce, dormice can enter torpor, a short period of deep sleep that saves energy. Researchers think warmer summers may mean less time in torpor and leave dormice with more energy to feed and breed. The animals may also have a better chance to build up fat reserves before winter. One ecologist who worked on the survey says it is still unclear how dormice will respond to warmer, wetter winters. People working to save wildlife say looking after the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live is essential to their long-term survival.

advanced.headline: Hazel dormice show signs of recovery in England and Wales
advanced.brief: Hazel dormouse numbers show tentative signs of recovery after decades of decline. The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the People’s Trust for Endangered Species, has monitored sites in England and Wales since 1998. Its data indicate that dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60 per cent since 2000, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5 per cent. Although the monitoring data point to a possible increase of nearly 10 per cent between 2020 and 2025, researchers stress that there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate. The apparent upturn coincided with springs and summers that were warmer and drier than average. Hazel dormice typically hibernate from around October to May, spending the winter in nests on the ground. In spring and summer, cold, wet weather or a shortage of food can prompt dormice to enter torpor, a short spell of deep sleep that conserves energy. Warmer summers may reduce the need for torpor and leave dormice with more energy for feeding and reproduction, researchers suggest. Ecologist Charlotte Armitage cautioned that it remains unclear how warmer, wetter winters might affect dormice. The researchers say the potential longer-term effects of climate change on the species warrant further investigation. Once widespread, the hazel dormouse is now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. Hazel dormice have become much rarer amid widespread woodland loss, and native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties. Conservationists stress that safeguarding the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.
